plays.author: sophocles
plays.title: Antigone
plays.proposed_subject: Antigone with her hands bound, brought before Creon (John, 2026-10-02)
plays.status: Drawn 2026-10-02/03 (second session), redrawn from John's traces. John, 2026-10-03: 'Antigone looking pretty good'
plays.credit: After the Apulian red-figure amphora of Panathenaic shape by the Darius Painter, c. 350-320 BCE, from Ceglie del Campo, Berlin, Antikensammlung F 3240 (RVAp 18/23), body A, upper frieze: Antigone with her hands bound, led by a guard, before Heracles and Creon. Photograph: ArchaiOptix (Commons file _04; files _05 and _06 used only to fit the vase's shape). Drawing traced from the photograph and changed.
plays.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photos by ArchaiOptix; Commons file pages checked 2026-10-02). The drawing is a derivative and is released under CC BY-SA 4.0 with this credit. The file pages add that some museums permit photography for non-commercial use only; that is a note, not a licence term.
plays.crop: Antigone alone, cut along her own outline: the guard and his spear, the boy, Heracles and Creon left out; the guard's cord, which only touches her wrists, goes with him. Both feet kept, the back one half under her hem. Two mended breaks (across her upper arm and across her skirt) are erased whole; the folds they broke are joined across, on the arm along John's own trace.
plays.alt_text: Antigone, veiled, her hands bound behind her back, her head bowed
plays.shows: The play itself: Antigone brought before Creon after burying Polynices (Antigone 384 ff.), as the vase is usually read. Some scholars connect the vase with a lost Euripidean Antigone, in which Heracles intercedes for her; John ruled (2026-10-02) that the image goes to Sophocles' Antigone whatever play the vase was painted for.
plays.method: The vase's profile and the cameras of photos 04, 05 and 06 fitted together (tools/vase_unroll.py: the animal frieze's upper border in three photos, 06's outline, points matched between the photos; focal lengths from EXIF), the vase flattened without shear, and photo 04 laid onto it: her feet and lower skirt come out up to 13% taller than in the photo. Clay found by colour; painted lines by local contrast, redrawn as even lines at the house weight; in her head the lines are the paint itself thinned to its centres. Her hands and face from John's own traces (the hands once, the face three times, each closer), registered onto the frame by SIFT to within half a pixel; where his outline encloses paint, the paint is drawn filled; her eye is the paint itself, its strokes too close for outlines. The mends erased and their folds joined (the arm's from John's trace). tools/antigone.py.
plays.result: John, 2026-10-03, on the third pass: 'Antigone looking pretty good.' On the second pass: 'The clothes are good. But hands need more work as do the face'; he then traced the hands and the face himself, and the drawing follows his traces. The reddish streak across her cheek, which he marked, is not drawn ('the orange strokes don't translate to two tone'). Open, put to John: a small dark spot on her upper arm, kept because the vase paints it; her jaw and chin drawn as two close lines, with clay between them in dark mode (one line instead?). A faint clay fringe along long straight edges in dark mode comes from the shared tracer and is flagged separately.

plays.author: sophocles
plays.title: Oedipus Tyrannus
plays.proposed_subject: Oedipus from the Syracuse krater, read as a scene from the play (the messenger's news); chosen by John 2026-10-02 over the Sphinx scene, which the play only alludes to.
plays.status: Drawn 2026-10-02: usable
plays.credit: After the Sicilian red-figure calyx-krater attributed to the Capodarso Painter, c. 330-320 BCE, Syracuse, Museo Archeologico Regionale "Paolo Orsi" 66557 (excavated at Syracuse, 1968-69); drawn from Dan Diffendale's photograph (Rome, Ara Pacis exhibition, 2024) and changed: cut out, cracks removed, staff redrawn as a straight rod, hair and beard drawn solid, hand redrawn, redrawn as line.
plays.license: Source photo CC BY-NC-SA 2.0 (Flickr licence of the exact file, checked 2026-10-02). The drawing traces only the ancient painting, which is public domain, so it does not carry the photo's licence (John, 2026-10-02: the vase's image is not copyrighted even if the photo is); the photo is credited.
plays.crop: Oedipus alone, cut out of the scene. Left out: the old messenger and the boy at left, the girl and the column at right, Jocasta, the stage floor, and the modern plaster fill by his elbow.
plays.alt_text: Oedipus, bearded, in a long embroidered robe, his hand at his beard, holding a staff
plays.shows: The play itself, as usually read (Taplin, Pots and Plays no. 22): the moment the Corinthian messenger's news lands, with Jocasta and the daughters beside him.
plays.method: Red-figure photo: a loose cut through the glaze (wide glaze joined to the background is left out), hand-drawn zones for the stage floor, the plaster fill, his shoes, and his head; three cracks erased and the lines they broke rejoined; a fourth crack, mended with grey plaster beside his hand, erased whole along John's outline of it, with nothing drawn along it: the lines it broke are joined across it (his hand's edges after John's trace, his robe's folds carried to his sleeve). It was first drawn as the staff, then as the edge of his sleeve; John, 2026-10-02: 'it looks like damage to the vase', 'The outlines of the crack need to be gone', 'Draw the lines so as to fill in the parts missing due to the crack'; below his sleeve the flaked staff redrawn as a straight rod on its painted centre line. Head revised after John's review (2026-10-02, 'crude and not refined'): the hair, a mass of tiny curls, drawn solid with its curly outline; the beard, whose strokes are too dense to hold apart at the house line weight, drawn solid with its long clay strands kept as light lines (John asked for a fuller beard); his hand at his beard redrawn stroke by stroke after John's trace of it (each stroke on a painted line read from Diffendale's second, sharper photo, or on John's trace where the paint is worn or under the restored patches), each finger a closed outline along its painted edges, with the black ground between two fingertips filled (John: 'Get the outlines. It's a line drawing'); the face lines redrawn as even lines along their centres. Lines by local contrast; painted lines broken by wear joined across their gaps where two line ends face each other (John: 'fill in the gaps of the lines where damage has erased parts'); more worn folds joined by hand, each checked against the photo (John: 'Do the folds but not hem and shoes'), and folds of the lower robe worn to faint dashes carried on where the photo still shows the dashes (found with a ridge filter, each checked by eye); the long crack across his robe re-placed onto the crack itself, whose dark line had been traced as a fold; the edge of his forearm drawn down from the wrist across the crack after John's trace; house line weight; potrace. tools/oedipus_syracuse.py.
plays.result: Usable. Revised: hair and beard solid, face lines even, the hand redrawn after John's trace with every finger outlined, the mended crack beside it gone, and lines broken by wear joined. The robe folds are sharp; the hem and the shoes are worn on the vase and stay rough; the shoes are drawn as solid black shapes.

plays.author: sophocles
plays.title: Philoctetes
plays.proposed_subject: Philoctetes alone on Lemnos, seated on a rock, his bandaged leg drawn up, his bow case at his feet (John, 2026-10-03: the Met lekythos is 'for philoctetes').
plays.status: Drawn 2026-10-03, sixth pass: head, feet and hands from John's traces, half tone on hair and beard
plays.credit: After the Attic red-figure squat lekythos in the manner of the Eretria Painter (Bothmer; BAPD 10931), c. 420 BCE, New York, Metropolitan Museum of Art 56.171.58 (Fletcher Fund, 1956): Philoctetes seated on a rock under a tree. Photographs: Marie-Lan Nguyen, 2011 (Commons), and the Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access, DP165159 and DP165160). Drawing traced from the photographs and changed.
plays.license: Nguyen's photo CC BY 2.5 (Commons file page, checked 2026-10-03); the Met's photos CC0 (Open Access; the object record says isPublicDomain: true). The drawing traces only the ancient painting, which is public domain, so it carries no licence (John's ruling on Oedipus Tyrannus, 2026-10-02; on this drawing, 2026-10-03: 'Don't care about license'); the photographers are credited.
plays.crop: Philoctetes with the rock he sits on and his bow case (John, 2026-10-03: 'include quiver and bow and the rock'), cut out as one. The tree is cut off where its trunk meets the rock, along the rock's top line and the top of his right hand. The black ground seen through the scene (between his arms and his body, under his raised leg and foot, between his hanging leg and the rock) stays open. The rock is its outline and its black lines only; its brown washes are left out.
plays.alt_text: Philoctetes alone on Lemnos, seated on a rock, his bandaged leg drawn up, his bow case beside him
plays.shows: The play itself: Philoctetes alone on Lemnos with his wound and the bow, where the Greeks left him, the situation the play opens on. Not a myth the play only mentions.
plays.method: The vase's profile and the cameras of the three photos fitted together (tools/vase_unroll.py: the vase's outline in the Met's two views, the line under the scene in all three, points matched between the photos; Nguyen's focal length from EXIF, the Met's fitted: fixed anywhere from 9,000 to 34,000 px it moves the flat figure by 2-3 px). The vase flattened without shear over the scene alone (it wraps 150 degrees round the vase), which keeps every part within 3% of the vase's own lengths; the photos laid onto it, Nguyen's in the middle and the Met's DP165159 toward the sides, where it is sharper. Him, the rock and the bow case found by colour as one cut-out, the tree cut off along the rock's own top line; the outline drawn on the clay's edge (not the browner stripe of glaze the painter laid along it) and smoothed along its length. Painted lines found by their narrowness, so the broad brown washes drop out, and redrawn as even lines at the house weight; faint and worn lines joined across their gaps; on the rock only black lines, on the bow and bow case all of them; the bow's faint outer top curve and the outer line round the end of the strap's loop placed by hand on the paint. His head from John's own trace (registered onto the frame by SIFT, 0.3 px): his strokes as lines, his filled marks (eye, brow, the marks at his neck) solid, the black top of the head solid with the fillet he outlined left light; his hair and beard carry a half tone (a third path in the line colour at 30% opacity) where the vase has its brown wash. His feet from his trace too (0.45 px): his strokes as lines, the dark bands he traced on both edges filled; the broad dark stroke down the back of his raised calf, first taken for ground seen through, drawn as paint; the ground seen between his legs drawn black on the light page too. His hands from his traces as well (0.25-0.27 px): his single lines replace the lines found along the painted strokes, and the figure's edge reaches out to his contour. The bow case's black and the dark strokes outlining his feet drawn solid. A scratch and an abraded patch in the glaze by his arm, and chips along the rock's left side, left out of the outline. tools/philoctetes.py.
plays.result: Sixth pass, 2026-10-03. John on the first: 'It needs to be refined. Not all the dark ink on the quiver and arrow are captured'; 'part of the top outside curve of the bow isn't drawn' (fixed in the second and third passes). He then traced the head himself, and asked for a half tone on the beard ('a half-dark tone for the beard to mimic the tone of the original on the beard') and the hair ('same for hair'), then lighter ('the original wasn't just a different tone but also somewhat less opaque': 45% to 30%). He also caught the strap loop's outer line missing at its end ('you also missed part of the strap'). Then he traced the feet, and marked the stroke down his raised calf and the end of his raised sole's band as black ('blue shows where the black should be'), and the ground between his legs ('Fill those in with black. They look weird not black in day mode.'); the gaps by his arms stay white on the light page (his pick). Then he traced the hands.

plays.author: sophocles
plays.title: Oedipus at Colonus
plays.proposed_subject: Blind Oedipus at the altar between his daughters, Ismene and Antigone, from the Apulian krater Taplin reads as a scene from the play (Pots & Plays no. 27); the three on the altar chosen by John 2026-10-02, over Oedipus alone.
plays.status: Drawn 2026-10-03: approved by John ("Merge.") and merged into claude/redesign-drawings
plays.credit: After the Apulian red-figure calyx-krater close to the De Schulthess Painter, 340s BCE, formerly Melbourne, Graham Geddes collection A 5:8; drawn from the photographs in J. R. Green, Ancient Voices, Modern Echoes: Theatre in the Greek World (Nicholson Museum, University of Sydney, 2003), pp. 4, 26 and 29 (HathiTrust mdp.39015060089391), with the painted lines and borders outside p. 26 (Ismene, the altar's left end, the strip along the bottom) from a photo of the scene found online (source unknown), placed on the same photo as reprinted in Oliver Taplin, Pots & Plays (Getty, 2007), no. 27, p. 101 ("From Green 2003, p. 4"), checked against the photo in Digital LIMC (monument 8378, photo 8569X101, © Graham Geddes Collection (once)), and changed: cut out, columns and tripods left out, redrawn as line, the daughters' faces, Antigone's hand and forearm, and Oedipus' lower fingers drawn after John Boyer's traces and marks.
plays.license: The found photo's source and terms are unknown (John, 2026-10-03: "don't worry about the credit"). The other source photos are in copyright: Green 2003 (the HathiTrust scan is under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0), its reprint in Taplin 2007, and the Digital LIMC photo (CC BY-NC 4.0 on the LIMC site). The drawing traces only the ancient painting, which is public domain, so it carries no licence from any of them (John, 2026-10-02: "The vase's image ISN'T copyrighted even if the photo IS"; the Syracuse drawing set the same rule for a CC BY-NC-SA photo); the photos are credited.
plays.crop: Oedipus seated on the altar between Ismene (left) and Antigone (right), with the altar, cut out of the scene. Left out: the two Ionic columns behind the altar and their tripods, the bearded king at far left (Creon for Taplin), the youth at far right (Polynices), the Erinys above, the boukranion, platters and festoons.
plays.alt_text: Blind Oedipus, white-haired and bearded, seated at an altar with his staff, one hand raised, between his daughters Ismene and Antigone
plays.source_file: Drawn from: HathiTrust mdp.39015060089391 (Green 2003), page images seq 6 (p. 4, the whole vase, 1.8 times the plate's scale), seq 28 (p. 26, the right half of the scene, 6.4 times) and seq 31 (p. 29, Oedipus' head and hand, 12.8 times), TIFF, downloaded by John (2026-10-03): https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=mdp.39015060089391. Ismene's lines: a 547x560 photo of the scene John found online (2026-10-03; probably from a Facebook post, source unknown; kept locally as found.png), registered to the plate (SIFT, median error 0.42 of its px; local misfit over Ismene 0.1 plate px). Frame: https://media.getty.edu/Text/6f3674dd-413a-56da-bec2-9da5564907df.pdf, page 112 (book p. 101), the plate, a 942x641 JPEG at 150 dpi (pdfimages -j -f 112 -l 112); every hand-placed point is in its px. Checked against: Digital LIMC, monument 8378 (scene 8569), photo 8569X101, the whole vase in black and white, 2198x2519: https://iiif.dasch.swiss/080E/39p0GV9AZiB-7HG3RtcJ3N4.jpx/full/max/0/default.png (downloaded with John's OK, 2026-10-03), aligned to the plate and used to read shapes the plate blurs; the tool does not read it.
plays.shows: The play itself. Oedipus, blind, has taken refuge at the altar in the grove at Colonus, with Antigone, who shares his exile, and Ismene, who comes with news of his sons' war and of the oracle (lines 310-509). Taplin (Pots & Plays no. 27) argues that the scene can be read only by someone who knows Sophocles' play: the story belongs to Athens and was Sophocles' own, the king at left and the young man at right fit Creon and Polynices pulling Oedipus to opposite sides, and the Erinys above stands for the goddesses of the grove, on whom Oedipus calls when he curses Polynices.
plays.method: Red-figure photo -> line drawing, in a frame 4x the plate: the plate's crop cleaned of JPEG noise (non-local means) and enlarged 4x (Lanczos); Green's pages registered to it in a chain (plate to p. 4 to p. 26 to p. 29: SIFT matches, a RANSAC homography, then a thin-plate spline on what it leaves; median errors 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1 plate px), warped into the frame, colour-matched to the plate so its thresholds hold, and laid over it, p. 29 over p. 26, feathered at the seams. p. 4 only links the chain: its print noise traced as wiggles. Ismene's painted lines and the dark borders of her mantle, and the painted lines of the altar's left end and the strip below p. 26, are found on a clean photo of the scene John found online, registered to the plate the same way; its black glaze has sheen no colour match flattens, so the ground, the outline, the black and the white there still come from the plate. A speck of brown at the corner of Antigone's veil (which left a tiny loop of outline) is counted as ground, and a speck on the altar's white is not drawn (both found by the Codex review). A loose cut round the group and the altar; inside it the ground is the black glaze that reaches the cut, with the two white columns counted as ground; the brown band a blur leaves at each outline is peeled off, so each figure has one outline where the clay begins. Lines: the outline; the edges between the figures and the white altar; painted lines, dots and bands by local contrast, kept at their own widths; faint folds found with a ridge filter (Sato) and drawn as smooth strokes; dashes left by wear joined where two ends face each other; where painted lines lie closer than the line weight (the zigzag ends of the two mantles, the pleats at Oedipus' neckline, two folds by his hand) they are redrawn along their centres. Ismene's mantle borders and the daughters' dark hair drawn solid, with white beads and pale curls left as holes. Oedipus from p. 29: his face found by colour and closed by its lines, which are drawn by hand on the painted marks (brows, closed eyes tapered as heavy as the lashes, nose with its tip and nostril, both lips, the far cheek, the two white forehead wrinkles), with John's rough marks on that page as a guide; his white hair and beard outlined, with the dark marks between the curls drawn solid, as John marked them in the beard ('the mouth and beard need more detail'); the staff in its two visible parts, each edge measured row by row (the lower part leans the other way, so it is not one rod; the hand covers its end, the hanging cloth its middle); the raised hand's outline taken from the clay's edge against the column, with the knuckle line and the wrist's edge; the two lower fingers as John marked them on p. 29 (the ring finger's edge round its tip, the line between the two, and the little finger's lower edge, meeting that line short of the ring finger's tip, as he asked: 'the ring finger here should be longer than the pinky'); the two raised fingers, about one plate px apart as painted, closed into one lump at the site's sizes ('Oedipus's hand does read as lump'), so each is turned a little about its base, away from the other (12 and 7 degrees). Ismene's face after John's trace over the plate (2026-10-03): his screenshot registered to the review sheet by SIFT (556 matches, 0.05 plate px) and each stroke carried back to the plate; her brow and eye as he marked them on the found photo ('Face could be better', 'She's not smiling'), a profile eye with its iris; then her profile from the nose down (the base of the nose, the lips, the chin) and a level mouth line from his second marks; the nose comes to a sharp angle with a straight, level underside, as he asked, the figure's edge cut to it there. Where one of his strokes runs along the outline the outline stands for it, and the pieces left just outside it are not drawn. Antigone after his two traces on p. 26 itself (2026-10-03: her face; her hand and forearm, with the armlet and the necklace's beads), made after the tool's own tracing of her fingers fell short: each screenshot matches the page 1:1 (SIFT, residual 0.04 and 0.02 page px), each stroke is carried to plate px through the page's registration, and the areas he filled (the irises, two dark spots between her fingertips, the heavier line at her elbow) stay solid; a thin rim of clay keeps her left iris apart from her hair. House line weight; potrace. tools/oedipus_colonus.py; a full run from the page files gives the same SVG as the cached frame.
plays.result: Third pass (2026-10-03), drawn from Green's pages and a photo John found: Oedipus' face, hair and beard, staff and hand follow the paint of p. 29 (his lower fingers John's marks, his raised fingers turned a little apart so they read at display size); Antigone follows John's traces on p. 26; Ismene's garment folds come from the found photo, her face from John's traces and marks. The zigzag ends of the two mantles are only as clear as the photos allow.

plays.status: Drawn in the phase 1 test, 2026-10-02: usable
plays.credit: After the Lucanian red-figure calyx-krater near the Policoro Painter, c. 400 BCE, Cleveland Museum of Art 1991.1, Leonard C. Hanna Jr. Fund; drawn from the museum's photograph of side A (alternate image 3, the full-resolution TIFF).
plays.license: CC0 (Cleveland Open Access record: share_license_status CC0, checked 2026-10-02)
plays.crop: Medea in the serpent chariot, cut out of the sun disk along the disk's own border. Kept: both netted sleeves (the left one's net pattern was first dropped as a hole). Left out: the Furies, Jason, the nurse, the teacher and the children's bodies on the altar below.
plays.alt_text: Medea in a chariot drawn by two serpents
plays.shows: The play itself: the museum ties the scene to Euripides' Medea. It shows the ending (her escape); the dead children are left out.
plays.method: Red-figure photo: clay found by brightness on a print-size copy, the disk border cut away per degree around its centre, the sleeve outlined by hand; inner lines from the full-resolution TIFF by local contrast with hysteresis; house line weight; potrace. tools/medea.py.
plays.result: Usable. Revised twice on 2026-10-02: the face shows eyelids, pupils, brows, nose and lips; the netted left sleeve is drawn; in dark mode the goad and the gaps inside the figure carry the clay. Still the busiest drawing; the serpents' painted spots come through.

plays.crop: Tried: the letter scene in view LC-31_11_2b: the messenger (in the Met's words, Agamemnon's slave) with the letter, and Menelaus 'taking the letter from the messenger by force'. Test file: docs/redesign/drawings/rejected/iphigenia-at-aulis.svg, not for use.
plays.shows: The play itself: the Met record describes five scenes from Euripides' Iphigenia at Aulis, with name inscriptions.
plays.method: XDoG, Canny at three scales and local-contrast thresholds found no usable lines in the worn low relief. A hand outline on a local-contrast copy gave featureless silhouettes. tools/iphigenia.py.
plays.result: Failed. The relief is too low and worn to trace from these photographs, and the Met lists no publication before 1933, so no old drawing is likely. Needs new raking-light photographs, a scholarly drawing whose licence allows reuse, or an original drawing from checked references. The second bowl of the series (ending with Iphigenia and Achilles) is a lead to check.

playwrights.author: aeschylus
playwrights.title: Aeschylus
playwrights.status: Drawn in the phase 1 test, 2026-10-02: clean
playwrights.credit: After Carl Bötticher's drawing (the plate is signed 'Gez. v. C. Boetticher') of the Apulian red-figure volute-krater by the Black Fury Painter, Naples, Museo Archeologico Nazionale: Orestes at Delphi. C. Bötticher, Der Omphalos des Zeus zu Delphi (Berlin, 1859), lithographed plate (Heidelberg page 10a). Scan: Heidelberg University Library.
playwrights.license: Public domain (published 1859). Heidelberg labels the scan with the Public Domain Mark 1.0 (IIIF manifest, checked 2026-10-02).
playwrights.crop: The Pythia only, cut along her own lines, with straight cuts across blank paper (between her hands and her head, above the fingertips of her raised left hand, under the lowest ruffles of her hem). Kept: both ends of her starred shawl, its lower edge and its black folds. Left out: Apollo, his N-patterned cloak, the laver behind her, the black Fury above. Apollo's raised back foot lies across her hem: its lines are erased, and her dress's black stripe is drawn on across the gap to the hem (45px at the scan's size, a straight continuation of the stripe; the rest of the hem there is left plain). That one line is a reconstruction, not in the engraving.
playwrights.alt_text: The Pythia, Apollo's priestess, fleeing in terror with her hands raised
playwrights.shows: Related to the play: Orestes at Delphi, the setting of the Eumenides' opening, where the Pythia comes out of the temple in terror (34 ff.). A painting of the myth, not a record of a performance. Identification: Classical Art Research Centre, Oxford, 'Black Fury painter's Orestes crater' (an old priestess 'flees in alarm'), https://www.carc.ox.ac.uk/carc/resources/Introduction-to-Greek-Pottery/Keypieces/apulian/orestes
playwrights.method: Engraved plate: ink by threshold with the paper tone divided out; cut by a least-cost path through hand-placed points; house line weight; potrace. tools/pythia.py.
playwrights.result: Clean. Revised 2026-10-02 after John's review: her right arm, the curl on top of her head, her left index finger and the whole shawl were added. The Commons copy of this plate is a blurred 1.5x upscale of the same scan; use the Heidelberg file.

playwrights.author: sophocles
playwrights.title: Sophocles
playwrights.proposed_subject: The shepherd Euphorbos carrying the infant Oedipus (John, 2026-10-02)
playwrights.status: Drawn 2026-10-02 (second session); redrawn after John's review. John, 2026-10-02, on the second round: 'You flattened it right to my eyes'
playwrights.credit: After the Attic red-figure neck-amphora by the Achilles Painter, c. 450-445 BCE, from Vulci, Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, Cabinet des médailles 372 (ARV² 987.4; BAPD 213824), side A: Euphorbos carrying the infant Oedipus, both named on the vase (ΕΥΦΟΡΒΟΣ, ΟΙΔΙΠΟΔΑΣ). Photographs: ArchaiOptix, 2023 (Commons files _01 to _04). Drawing traced from the photographs and changed.
playwrights.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (all four photos by ArchaiOptix; Commons file pages checked 2026-10-02). The drawing is a derivative and is released under CC BY-SA 4.0 with this credit. The file pages add that some museums permit photography for non-commercial use only; that is a note, not a licence term.
playwrights.crop: Euphorbos with the child, his spear at full length (John, 2026-10-02: first shortened, then 'longer spear please', then full length). The meander band he stands on is cut away along his soles; the inscriptions are left out. Above his belt the figure comes from photo 03, a close view from above that looks almost straight at his head; below, from photo 02, which faces him. Past his outline the spear is drawn straight, on one line fitted to the painted shaft on both sides of him, out to its butt spike (from photo 01) and blade (from photo 04), at the lengths the vase model gives. The back of his neck, which the vase leaves unmarked, is drawn in.
playwrights.alt_text: The shepherd Euphorbos carrying the infant Oedipus on his shoulder, a long spear in his hand
playwrights.shows: Backstory the play turns on: a shepherd, named Euphorbos on the vase, carrying the infant Oedipus, the rescue that the play's last revelation brings to light. Not a scene staged in the play. Chosen by John, 2026-10-02, as Sophocles' home-page figure.
playwrights.method: Four photographs, one drawing. The vase and the four cameras fitted together (tools/vase_unroll.py: a surface of revolution and pinhole cameras, from the silhouettes, the meander's lower edge, the ring at the base of the neck, and points matched between the photos; every photo's focal length fixed from its EXIF, the cropped photos' centres fitted). The vase then flattened as rigidly as it allows, so every small patch keeps its shape. Above the belt the drawing comes from photo 03, which looks almost straight at the shoulder where his head is; below, from photo 02. Clay found by colour; painted lines by local contrast, redrawn as even lines at the house weight; the hand, the two faces and the left sandal drawn as hand-placed strokes snapped to the painted lines, the faces at a finer pen; hair and the cord on his back solid. The back of his neck drawn in where the vase has no line. tools/euphorbos.py.
playwrights.result: Two rounds on 2026-10-02; John on the second: 'You flattened it right to my eyes.' First: photo 02 unrolled by arc length; John found the head and upper body squashed ('like a Neanderthal') and the hat on his back growing out of his neck ('an insane tumor'). Cause: that unrolling shears whatever lies off its centre line where the vase's profile slopes (his face by about 8 degrees, the hat by 18), and the cameras' focal lengths had been fitted at twice their true value. Second: the shear-free flattening, the true focal lengths, the upper body from photo 03, and a line for the back of his neck (John asked for it). The head now matches photo 03, the view John pointed to, at matched scale. Open: the spear is drawn straight through his fist, though unrolled the painted shaft bends a few degrees there; a heavy dark wedge where his jaw meets the child's head; a faint clay fringe along long straight edges in dark mode comes from the shared tracer and is flagged separately.
playwrights.superseded: docs/redesign/drawings/sophocles-oedipus.svg (Oedipus before the Sphinx, Berlin F 2355, photo by Gary Todd, CC0): the phase 1 test. John found it too sparse, and the Sphinx scene misleading about the plot.

playwrights.author: euripides
playwrights.title: Euripides
playwrights.proposed_subject: A directly sourced scene from a surviving play
playwrights.status: Drawn in the phase 1 test, 2026-10-02: clean
playwrights.credit: After R. Jaene's lithograph (the plate is signed 'Lith. v. R. Jaene' and 'Druck aus R. Jaene's Kunst-Anst. in Berlin') of the Duke of Buckingham's vase, Archäologische Zeitung 7 (1849), Denkmäler und Forschungen, Taf. XII ('Iphigenia in Tauris. Vasenbild des Herzogs von Buckingham'), with O. Jahn's article. Scan: Internet Archive (Getty Research Institute copy), leaf n156.
playwrights.license: Public domain (published 1849). The Internet Archive item is marked 'Possible copyright status: NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT'.
playwrights.crop: Iphigenia with the whole tablet, the temple key, its chain and knob, and her right forearm down its outer edge. Left out: Pylades, the temple door and steps behind her (the cut follows her veil's curve, not the door's straight edge), Artemis' foot, the attendant and her tray. At this scan's size Pylades' fingertips on the tablet's far edge cannot be told apart from it, so a few strokes there may be his.
playwrights.alt_text: Iphigenia, priestess of Artemis, holding out a letter tablet and the temple key
playwrights.shows: The play itself, as O. Jahn identifies the scene in the 1849 publication: Iphigenia handing her letter to Pylades (Iphigenia in Tauris 727 ff.). Jahn records that Welcker read it the other way round, with Iphigenia receiving the letter. The vase's present location was not checked.
playwrights.method: Lithograph: fine grey lines found by local contrast with hysteresis (ink_lines); least-cost cut; house line weight; potrace. tools/iphigenia_tauris.py.
playwrights.result: Clean. Revised twice on 2026-10-02 after John's review: her right forearm, key hand, chain, sandals, veil edge and the whole tablet are in.

playwrights.proposed_subject: A comic actor or checked comedy reference
playwrights.status: Drawn in the phase 1 test, 2026-10-02: clean
playwrights.credit: After the Apulian red-figure bell-krater by the Schiller Painter, ca. 370 BCE, Würzburg, Martin von Wagner Museum H 5697 (RVAp 4/4a). Photograph: ArchaiOptix, CC BY-SA 4.0. Drawing traced from the photograph and changed.
playwrights.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photo by ArchaiOptix, checked 2026-10-02). The drawing is a derivative and is released under CC BY-SA 4.0 with this credit. The file page adds that some museums allow photography for non-commercial use only; that is a note, not a licence term.
playwrights.crop: The old woman only, read as Mika (the play's First Woman, called Mikka at 760; the Commons record says 'old woman with skyphos'). The blade of Mnesilochus' knife, which touches her bowl's rim, is cut away along the blade's edge; Mnesilochus, on the altar, is left out.
playwrights.alt_text: Mika, in a comic old woman's mask, holding out a bowl
playwrights.shows: The play itself, as the vase is read: the mock sacrifice of the wineskin 'baby' in Women at the Thesmophoria, staged as a phlyax play. Mika asks for a bowl to catch its blood at 754-755 (the repo's Hall-Geldart text, where she is the First Woman, called Mikka at 760).
playwrights.method: Red-figure photo: clay found by brightness; fold lines by local contrast with hysteresis (ink_lines); knife cut; house line weight; potrace. tools/mika.py.
playwrights.result: Clean. Revised 2026-10-02: the drapery folds run their full length. John judged the first version not detailed enough; the Schiller Painter's own drawing is sparer than the engravings.

drawing_format: Each SVG is 1000 units tall with two paths: 'lines' (fill currentColor) and 'body', the figure's area under the lines, class "body" with fill="none", which a page fills with CSS. The body has no holes, except where a scene shows the black ground through it (Philoctetes: between his arms and his body), and lines too thin to hold clay on either side (a goad, a spear) get a narrow clay rim, so the figure reads whole on a dark page. Light pages leave the body transparent; the contact sheet's dark boards fill it with clay and keep the lines dark, as on a red-figure vase (approved by John 2026-10-02; the inverted dark mode looked like a photo negative).
